Several sources of uncertainty could cause outcomes to land outside even these relatively wide intervals. Macroeconomic data surprises, such as an unexpected inflation print, employment report, or central bank policy shift, could generate sharp moves that push prices well beyond the stated bounds. Geopolitical shocks, liquidity events, or financial contagion from other markets could produce discontinuous jumps that historical volatility models systematically underestimate. On the upside, a sudden shift in risk sentiment or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices significantly above the upper bound.

It is also worth acknowledging the model risk embedded in these forecasts. The intervals were constructed using assumptions about volatility and distribution that may not hold if the underlying regime changes. Fat-tailed distributions, which are empirically common in financial markets, mean that events outside a 90% confidence interval occur more frequently than naive Gaussian models would suggest. Practically speaking, roughly one in ten observations should fall outside this range under ideal conditions, but in stressed market environments that frequency can be considerably higher.
